en: The True Eye of the Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang Dynasty;
expounded by DAWEN, a later scholar of Wulin.
To explain this sutra, it is divided into eleven major sections: (1) explaining the title; (2) those who are able to practice;

(3) clarifying the essence of Prajñā; (4) clarifying the function of Prajñā; (5) correctly demonstrating the method of the three contemplations; (6) receiving that all dharmas are fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing;
(7) describing that within emptiness there are fundamentally no dharmas; (8) attaining through non-attainment; (9) praising the profundity.
The *Prajñā* [section] explains the ten secrets of *prajñā*. △ First, the explanation of the title:
*Prajñāpāramitāhṛdayasūtra*.

Master Tiantai once explained the titles of all sutras by means of five chapters: name (*ming*), essence (*ti*), doctrine (*zong*), function (*yong*), and the characteristics of the teaching (*jiaoxiang*).
In this sutra, the name consists of six characters consisting of both dharma and metaphor; the Sanskrit for these translates here as "Wisdom Reaching the Other Shore" (*prajñāpāramitā*).

This is the dharma, while the single character "mind" (*citta*) is the metaphor. Within *prajñā*, there are three aspects: the real mark (*lakṣaṇa*), contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), and letters (*vyañjana*).

The essence of the real mark is such that saints and ordinary beings are equal, and birth and Buddhahood are one and the same; each is perfectly complete, lacking not even a single thread of deficiency.
The dharmakāya, which is originally without beginning, is shrouded by ignorance and thus wanders through the five paths of rebirth.

By using the function of contemplative observation to illuminate and shatter all phenomena, one realizes that they are entirely empty in their very substance and are from the outset free of obstruction;
thus one immediately ascends to the other shore and sits in the realization of Bodhi. True reality is the dharmakāya, contemplative observation is prajñā, and reaching the other shore is liberation.
To be liberated from the secret treasury of the Three Virtues is not to depart from the person; it requires a single moment of direct realization before the mind can attain its core.
This is to extract the essence and the most refined essentials, serving as the sovereign that unifies the body, the four limbs, and the hundred bones.

Because this brief text encompasses the full meaning of the eight divisions and seven hundred volumes, it is said thus. With *bhūtatathatā* (the true aspect) as its substance, it is the foundation of all Mahāyāna.
Since all Mahayana sutras take the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as their essence, they take the illumination and vision of the emptiness of the aggregates (*skandha-śūnyatā*) as their thesis;

since they employ wisdom to shatter all phenomena, they take the transcendence of suffering as their function, swiftly surmounting the two kinds of birth-and-death. Thus, "ripe butter" serves as the characteristic of the teaching, for it is the vanguard of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
As for "sutra," it means "constant" and "dharma"; it is the constant path of sages and worthies that transcends the mundane dust.
The rules for its construction, including the threading and binding, are as described in detail elsewhere.
△ Second, regarding the practitioner, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva:
the Tathāgata, by citing the person who practices through the perfect and sudden realization, provides an exemplary model to encourage all ordinary and Hinayana practitioners.
When all phenomena are arrayed before one, one is not obstructed by any single emotion nor does one dwell in any single dharma.
Not abiding on either bank of the middle stream, one ascends to the other shore from this very shore. With unconditioned compassion, one responds universally to the myriad capacities of beings;
there is no land where one does not appear, like the moon reflected in a thousand rivers. Therefore, it is called "Sovereignty. △ Third, clarifying the essence of Prajñā.
"When practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*":
this refers to the essence of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), which is the virtuous conduct of the *dharmakāya*. "Profound" (*gambhīra*) distinguishes it from mere understanding without practice;

it distinguishes it from the mundane and heterodox, from the partial truth of the two vehicles, and from the provisional teachings of the "Middle" (the *tathatā-madhyama*). Because the three contemplations are unified within a single mind, it is called "profound."
At the moment of perfect understanding, one contemplates and follows along with contemplation, immediately realizing the timelessness of time; this distinguishes it from gradual progression.
△ Fourth, clarifying the function of Prajñā:
"To perceive that the five aggregates are all empty, and thereby transcend all suffering and calamity."

This clarifies the actual efficacy of profound Prajñā. Because these two virtues of Prajñā and liberation employ the power of perfect illumination to shine upon and penetrate everything until it is thoroughly seen, it is said:

"Illuminating and seeing that sentient beings take the root-body and the vessel-world—these manifestations of duality—as real, and through the grasping of name-and-form, they experience the agreeable, the disagreeable, and that which is neither, thereby giving rise to suffering."
Delighting in the Middle Way is called *vedanā* (feeling). The movement of deluded emotions, their grasping at objects, and their calculating deliberations are called *saṃjñā* (perception).

Their constant, subtle shifting and the incessant renewal of states such that nothing remains still are called *saṃskāra* (volitional formations). The clear and distinct discrimination of these is called *vijñāna* (consciousness). These five [aggregates] cover the true nature and obstruct the wondrous clarity; they constitute the *skandhas*.
Although the two vehicles have shattered the attachment to a self, their attachment to dharmas still persists; this is the sequential progression of the provisional vehicle.
Gradual severance has not yet reached its ultimate conclusion; the Bodhisattva, using the light of great wisdom, traces back to the source and finds no trace of coming or going.
Since there was never any delusion from the outset and the fundamental nature is inherently empty and quiescent, what need is there to dissect its substance?

Originally, there is no sudden transcendence of the distinctions between the six paths and four modes of birth, nor of the transformations resulting from long eons of diligent toil. Therefore it is said:
All the hardships and afflictions of the profound and subtle Prajñā have been fully disclosed here;
this is merely a reiteration for the sake of those who are ready to receive the teaching, serving as a commentary. △ Fifth, the formal instruction on the practice of the three contemplations:
"O Śāriputra, form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form; form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form. Feeling..."
The same applies to perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Śāriputra is the foremost in wisdom among the assembly; as he is the one suited to this occasion, the Tathāgata calls him by name and addresses him:

"Form is not different from emptiness"—this is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), which destroys the attachments of ordinary people and non-Buddhists regarding the reality of the sense bases (*āyatana*) and sense objects (*viṣaya*).
That this form gives rise to delusion and creates karma is truly the root of birth and death; therefore, it is explained:
"This grasped form is not different from true emptiness—do not remain attached to it. That emptiness is not different from form is the provisional contemplation (*prajñapti-darśana*).
Although those of the Two Vehicles use the emptiness of analytical destruction to break through that provisional form, they still cling to a biased emptiness.
For the sake of Nirvana, he instructs them, saying: "This emptiness that is realized is not different from conventional form;
do not grasp at the realization itself. Form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form—this is the Middle Way.

Fearing that those of the provisional vehicle, upon hearing they are "not different," will ultimately treat them as two distinct things—failing to understand that wisdom and the object are fused and identical, and thus still maintaining a sense of duality—he says this.
Because of the two views of emptiness and existence, he explained it thus: "The color of wondrous existence is itself the true mark of ultimate emptiness;
the emptiness of the true mark is itself true color. Therefore, this is called the Great Emptiness, the Emptiness of the Primary Meaning (paramārtha-śūnyatā).
Why should one not transcend birth and death? Why should one not be delivered from suffering and calamity? These words were not revealed all at once, nor were they recorded in successive volumes.
In the true Prajñāpāramitā, the Bodhisattva’s three contemplations are one mind, and the three truths are one object.

Since form (*rūpa*) is the foremost of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), form is explained in detail while the others are abbreviated. To speak exhaustively, sensation (*vedanā*) is not different from emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and emptiness is not different from sensation;

sensation is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself sensation. The same applies to perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). These three are likewise so.
△ 6. Upholding the Fundamental Nature of All Dharmas as Neither Arising nor Ceasing:
Śāriputra, the mark of emptiness of all dharmas is that they are neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.
This reiterates and clarifies the principle from the preceding text—that form and emptiness are not different—and demonstrates it:

that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are precisely the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) and the mark of ultimate truth (*lakṣaṇa*). As stated in the eighty-one sections of this work, "all phenomena" refers to both mundane and supramundane things.
These phenomena have never arisen from the beginning, nor do they undergo cessation; birth and death are themselves *nirvāṇa*, for they have never existed from the very start.
What need is there even to purify defilements? Afflictions are themselves bodhi; wisdom neither increases nor do delusions decrease.
The quiescence of all phenomena is itself true emptiness—what arising and ceasing, what defilement and purity, what increase and decrease could there be?
These six "nots" are simply the single word "emptiness. To speak of them fully: not coming, not going, not ceasing, not permanent...
The same applies to [the concepts of] non-identity, non-difference, non-existence, non-non-existence, and so forth. △ Seventh, it is described that within emptiness there is fundamentally no dharma;
therefore, within emptiness there is no form, no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; and no forms.
There is no eye constituent, nor even no mind-consciousness constituent;

there is no ignorance, nor the extinction of ignorance, and so on up to no old age and death, nor the extinction of old age and death; there is no suffering, origin, cessation, or path; there is no wisdom and no attainment.
This describes the establishment that within the empty characteristic of all phenomena, there is fundamentally no arising or ceasing;
not only is there no arising or ceasing, but within the essence of the true reality of ultimate emptiness, there are fundamentally no eighty-one categories of phenomena, mundane or supramundane.
Therefore, it is said that within the empty characteristic of all phenomena, there are fundamentally no five aggregates, nor the six sense organs such as the eye, nor the six objects such as form.
The six consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness and so forth, constitute the eighteen *dhātus* (elements), each having its own distinct lineage and boundary;

therefore, these do not pertain to worldly phenomena. From ignorance (*avidyā*) to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) is the gate of the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) in its forward progression, which is the object of contemplation for those who follow the path of the *pratyekabuddha*.
From the exhaustion of ignorance to the exhaustion of old age and death is the twelve links of dependent origination in its process of cessation.
The gateway is wisdom; when ignorance is severed and exhausted, then everything is exhausted.

Suffering and its Accumulation are the causes and effects of the mundane world, while Cessation and the Path are the causes and effects of the supramundane. These are what the Śrāvaka knows: he recognizes suffering, severs accumulation, aspires for cessation, and cultivates the path.
However, when the Bodhisattva contemplates them with wisdom, he sees that within the essence of the true mark of the ultimate emptiness of all phenomena, there is fundamentally no duality.
The Dharma cultivated and realized through the vehicles likewise lacks the wisdom of the Bodhisattvas of the *zang*, *tong*, and *bie* [teachings] to sever delusions;
there is no bodhi to be attained, no realization, and no attainment, for these are of provisional meaning and are all mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
This is not a supramundane Dharma. △ Eight: Attainment through Non-Attainment.
Because there is nothing to be apprehended, the Bodhisattva relies on the Prajñāpāramitā, and thus his mind is without hindrance.
Because he is without hindrance, he is free from fear; far removed from all inverted dreams and delusions, he attains ultimate Nirvāṇa.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time rely on the Prajñāpāramitā and thereby attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Regarding the three types of Bodhi:
the former [approach] uses the water of the wisdom of emptiness to wash away clinging attachments, the subtle and the coarse, the entanglements, and the four propositions;
it is what is meant by "merely exhausting ordinary sentiments, with no separate 'saintly understanding. One sweeps until there is nothing further to sweep.

Abiding in detachment until reaching the state where detachment itself is transcended, the fundamental essence is the True Buddha as suchness, which from the beginning has never moved even a hair’s breadth.
It is like the moon appearing when water is clear; rest is itself Bodhi.

Only then does one realize that previously, at every turn, one had missed the mark. This can be called non-cultivation being true cultivation, non-attainment being true attainment, and non-realization.

This is the true realization; therefore it is said that "because there is nothing to be attained," by relying on this true mark of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one reaches the other shore of *nirvāṇa* without obstruction.
How is it possible to reach it? Because one does not dwell in any single dharma and does not stagnate in any single emotion, the mind is immediately unimpeded;
being unimpeded is precisely what is meant by sovereignty (*svatantra*). Since there is no impediment, what fear could there be?
If one dwells in attachment, there is no self-mastery, and thus immeasurable fears and terrors arise.
Taking the impermanent to be permanent and suffering to be pleasure—these eight kinds of inversions—result in thoughts and mental activity by day and various dreams by night;
clinging to false objects, there is no time of rest. Throughout the long night of birth and death, there will never be a time of liberation.
To speak of it as one who is to be pitied, by means of this true emptiness one attains this true reality (*dharmatā*).
How could one be so sovereign as to forever leave behind all terror? How could there be any inverted delusions that are not abandoned?

Can this not be called the sudden realization of the ultimate state on the other shore of *nirvāṇa*? Whether they be Bodhisattvas who are persons of the cause or Buddhas who are persons of the fruit, there are none who do not rely upon this.
Through *prajñā*, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—this refers to the progression from cause to the stage of fruition.
That the fruit of bodhi-wisdom and the fruit of the cessation of *nirvāṇa* are mutually present or absent is an abbreviated or partial explanation. △ Ninth:
Praising Profound *Prajñā*.
Therefore, know that the Prajñāpāramitā is a great divine mantra, a great illuminating mantra, an unsurpassed mantra, a mantra equal to the unequaled;
it is able to eliminate all suffering, being true and not false.
This praise for the inconceivable meaning of Prajñāpāramitā is as follows: its "spirit" (*yi*) is the unfathomable numinous awareness;
its "clarity" (*ming*) is the brilliant mirror that penetrates and illuminates the darkness with the torch of wisdom. It is the swift vessel for crossing the ocean of suffering;
therefore, it is all called "Great. This Dharma is most honored and unsurpassed; throughout the nine realms and among the three vehicles, there is nothing equal to it, yet it is equal to all.
The mantra of the ultimate, supreme One Vehicle extols this Dharma as being beyond the reach of thought and speech;
how could it be encompassed by any measure? Since its meaning differs from that of lower mantras, it can eliminate the suffering of the two kinds of birth-and-death.
How could one not believe the true words spoken by the Tathāgata, which are entirely free from falsehood? This is clearly evident.
Having finished the explicit exposition of Prajñā, what follows is the secret exposition of Prajñā; this may be called the perfect integration of the Exoteric and Esoteric.
△ Tenth, because it is a secret exposition of Prajñā, he speaks the mantra of the Prajñāpāramitā, which is spoken as follows: *gate gate pāragate*...
The mantra *Tatpārasaṃgate Bodhi Svāhā* is the secret, ultimate exposition;
like a king’s confidential decree or a military command, how could it be permitted to leak out?
In the Exoteric Teachings, one hears and understands it, practices accordingly, and thereby attains the fruit; in the Esoteric Teachings, one receives and upholds it with reverence.
Because its profound benefit is bestowed beyond all possibility of explanation, it was not translated; this is the "secret non-translation" among the five reasons for not translating.
*The True Eye of the Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom* (End).
Within my old chest, I have a single scroll of the *Hannya Shingyō Shōgen* (Heart Sūtra Commentary on the True Eye) annotated with Japanese readings for circulation in the world.
Should anyone read it, may they, through the words, give rise to contemplation and illumination, thereby realizing the true nature (*bhūtatathatā*). Herein I record my aspiration for others.
Merely paper. Submitted by Zhikong of Luoxia.
